note: ORDER 283 — kriserna, engelska (översättning och nya steg av Claude Code).

somm-k1.title: A bad review
somm-k1.body: Aftontidningen has published a critical review of the wine list. Every guest in your part of town has read it.

steps.question: What does a reviewer usually judge a wine list on?

a.label: Whether it suits the food and the place, and whether the staff can explain it
a.explanation: A list is judged as part of the meal: how well the wines fit the food and the room, and how well the staff can guide the guest.

b.label: Only how many bottles are on it
b.explanation: A long list is not a good list in itself. Length without guidance can make choosing harder.

c.label: Only the price of the dearest bottle
c.explanation: One expensive bottle says little about the list the guests actually drink from.

fail.outcome: {personal} cannot say what the review was about. Guests start to wonder.

steps.question: A guest mentions the review at the table. How do you answer?

a.label: Listen, thank them, and say briefly what you are doing about it
a.explanation: Calm, open answers show that the team takes guests and critics seriously. It turns an awkward moment into trust.

b.label: Pretend you have not read it
b.explanation: The guest has read it. Pretending not to have seen it looks evasive.

c.label: Say the reviewer knows nothing about wine
c.explanation: Attacking the reviewer makes the guest take the criticism more seriously, not less.

fail.outcome: The guest feels brushed off and the table goes quiet.

steps.question: How does the team respond to the criticism professionally?

a.label: Cut prices at once
a.explanation: Lower prices do not answer criticism of the list, and they cost you margin.

b.label: Replace the whole list
b.explanation: Throwing out the list admits more than the review said and loses what worked.

c.label: Ignore the review
c.explanation: Silence leaves the review as the only story people hear.

d.label: Invite the journalist to a new tasting and show what you can do
d.explanation: An open dialogue and demonstrated skill turn bad press into good visibility. Speaking up first is the sommelier team's strongest tool.

fail.outcome: The review stands unanswered, and fewer guests book this week.

success.outcome: The journalist comes back, tastes, and writes a short follow-up. Guests notice.

staff.outcome: {personal} handles the questions as best they can, but the review is still what people talk about.

somm-k2.title: Supplier crisis
somm-k2.body: Your main wine supplier cannot deliver before the weekend's big dinner.

steps.question: Which wines are easiest to replace at short notice without changing the dinner?

a.label: Only wines of the same vintage
a.explanation: The vintage matters less than grape and style for keeping a pairing.

b.label: Wines of the same grape and style from another producer
b.explanation: The same grape and style keep the pairing's balance of acidity, body and sweetness, so the dishes still work.

c.label: Any wine at the same price
c.explanation: Price says nothing about acidity, body or sweetness, which decide whether the pairing works.

fail.outcome: {personal} picks replacements at random. Two of them clash with the food.

steps.question: What do you tell the guests who booked the dinner?

a.label: Nothing, and hope no one notices
a.explanation: Guests who booked a pairing notice. Finding out at the table feels like being misled.

b.label: Cancel the pairing and serve water
b.explanation: The guests booked a wine dinner. Cancelling is the worst outcome for them and for you.

c.label: Tell them before they arrive, name the replacements and why they fit
c.explanation: Telling guests early, with reasons, keeps their trust and turns a change into part of the story.

fail.outcome: The guests find out at the table and feel misled.

steps.question: Which option saves the evening best?

a.label: Close the restaurant
a.explanation: Closing loses the evening, the takings and the guests' trust.

b.label: Call a neighbouring team's sommelier and share a reserve stock
b.explanation: The sommelier network in Grythyttan is a resource. Working together in a crisis is practical and builds social sustainability in the long run.

c.label: Serve only beer
c.explanation: Beer can be good with food, but the guests booked a wine dinner.

d.label: Buy from Systembolaget at retail price
d.explanation: Buying at retail price wipes out the margin, and the right wines may not be in stock.

fail.outcome: The dinner goes ahead with gaps in the pairing, and the takings suffer.

success.outcome: The neighbours' reserve bottles save the dinner, and the guests hear how it was done.

staff.outcome: {personal} patches the pairing together. It works, but not well.

somm-k3.title: Extreme weather
somm-k3.body: A storm has damaged the harvest at your biodynamic supplier in Bergslagen. Prices are rising for everyone in the village.

steps.question: Why does a biodynamic grower have fewer quick fixes after storm damage?

a.label: Biodynamic vines are never damaged by weather
a.explanation: No farming method protects vines from storms.

b.label: The certification forbids harvesting after rain
b.explanation: There is no such rule. The limits are on what may be added, not when to pick.

c.label: Synthetic sprays and inputs are not allowed, so the grower relies on the vineyard's own resilience
c.explanation: Biodynamic farming rules out synthetic chemicals. After damage, the grower works with the living system rather than reaching for a spray.

fail.outcome: {personal} cannot explain the price rise to the guests.

steps.question: How do you adjust the wine list this week?

a.label: Remove every wine from the region at once
a.explanation: Dropping a partner at the first bad year loses a relationship you will want back.

b.label: Keep the grower's wines in smaller amounts and tell guests about the vintage
b.explanation: Keeping the relationship and telling the story of a hard vintage makes the scarcity part of what guests value.

c.label: Pour smaller glasses without saying so
c.explanation: Hidden cuts are noticed, and they cost more trust than a price rise.

fail.outcome: Guests notice smaller glasses and say so.

steps.question: Which answer is the most sustainable in the long run?

a.label: Raise the price of every dish
a.explanation: Passing the cost to everything hides the cause and hurts guests who never drink the wine.

b.label: Take the wine list off for now
b.explanation: A wine bar without a list has nothing to sell.

c.label: Switch to a cheaper conventional supplier
c.explanation: It solves this week and weakens your profile and your relationships for the years after.

d.label: Shorten the list and go deeper with fewer organic producers
d.explanation: A sustainable buying strategy is about depth rather than breadth. Fewer producers with strong relationships give resilience against climate disruption.

fail.outcome: The list gets cheaper and thinner, and regulars notice.

success.outcome: The grower thanks you for staying. Next year's allocation is yours.

staff.outcome: {personal} keeps the list going week by week, without a plan.

somm-k4.title: A VIP guest
somm-k4.body: A well-known food writer books a table tonight without warning. The whole village is talking about it.

steps.question: What does research on crossmodal correspondence show about music and taste?

a.label: Music has no effect on taste
a.explanation: Studies show that sound changes how we perceive taste, so the choice of music matters.

b.label: Music can change how sweet, bitter or rich a wine seems
b.explanation: Crossmodal research (Spence) shows that high, bright music can bring out sweetness and heavier music bitterness and astringency.

c.label: Only loud music affects taste
c.explanation: It is the character of the music, not only its volume, that matters.

fail.outcome: {personal} does not know why the room matters. The evening starts flat.

steps.question: How do you pace the service for a guest who is there to review?

a.label: Serve everything at once to show efficiency
a.explanation: Rushing a meal spoils it, however efficient it looks.

b.label: Keep the writer waiting to build anticipation
b.explanation: Waiting reads as poor service, not as drama.

c.label: The same pace as for every guest, just with care: no rushing, no hovering
c.explanation: A reviewer wants to see the real service. Care without special treatment is what they will write about.

fail.outcome: The writer notices the fuss, and so does everyone else.

steps.question: Which crossmodal strategy do you choose to make the most of the evening?

a.label: Serve the most expensive wine
a.explanation: Price is not the experience. The whole setting is.

b.label: Match music, light and pace to the character of the wines and the guest's expectations
b.explanation: The influence of the atmosphere, as Crichton-Fock (formerly Herdenstam) describes it: every sensory impression in the dining room works together. A thoughtful sommelier team orchestrates the whole, not just the glass.

c.label: Let the guest choose alone, without guidance
c.explanation: Guidance is part of the service being reviewed.

d.label: Focus only on the food
d.explanation: The wine and the room are half the experience.

fail.outcome: The evening is correct but forgettable.

success.outcome: The writer stays late, asks about the wines, and the village hears about it.

staff.outcome: {personal} takes the table. It goes well enough, but nothing stands out.

somm-k5.title: Short-staffed
somm-k5.body: Someone on the team is ill. One person has to handle all the wine service on a fully booked night.

steps.question: What does WSET SAT stand for?

a.label: A standard for serving temperatures
a.explanation: Temperatures matter, but SAT is about how to taste and judge a wine.

b.label: The Wine & Spirit Education Trust's Systematic Approach to Tasting
b.explanation: SAT is WSET's structured method: appearance, nose, palate and conclusions, in that order.

c.label: A sommelier aptitude test
c.explanation: It is a tasting method, not a test of the sommelier.

fail.outcome: {personal} fumbles the basics under pressure.

steps.question: Which tasting technique do you prioritise under time pressure?

a.label: Use WSET SAT — sight, smell, taste, conclusion — quickly but consistently
a.explanation: WSET SAT is designed for efficiency without losing precision. A trained sommelier makes a correct judgement in under 60 seconds.

b.label: Guess from the label
b.explanation: The label cannot tell you whether this bottle is sound.

c.label: Ask the head chef to taste
c.explanation: The kitchen is just as busy, and wine is the sommelier's job.

d.label: Skip tasting altogether
d.explanation: Without tasting, a corked or faulty bottle goes straight to the guest.

fail.outcome: A faulty bottle reaches a table before anyone notices.

steps.question: Halfway through the evening you cannot keep up. What do you prioritise?

a.label: Taste every wine thoroughly before pouring, whatever the queue
a.explanation: Thoroughness that leaves tables waiting helps no one tonight.

b.label: Let guests pour their own bottles from the bar
b.explanation: It gives up the service guests are paying for.

c.label: Tables still waiting for a first drink, then open bottles; tell the others honestly that they will wait a little
c.explanation: The first drink sets the evening for a table. Honesty about a short wait keeps the others' patience.

fail.outcome: Tables wait without a word, and the mood sinks.

success.outcome: One person keeps the whole room served, and the guests never notice the gap.

staff.outcome: {personal} runs between tables. Everyone gets something, late.

somm-k6.title: Sustainability audit
somm-k6.body: The municipality is reviewing every restaurant's environmental profile before the Sustainable Restaurant of the Year award.

steps.question: What makes up most of a wine's climate footprint?

a.label: The corks
a.explanation: Corks are a very small part of the footprint.

b.label: The serving temperature
b.explanation: Cooling uses energy, but far less than transport and glass.

c.label: Transport and packaging, above all heavy glass bottles
c.explanation: Transport and packaging dominate a wine's footprint; heavy glass is a large part of it.

fail.outcome: {personal} cannot answer the auditor's first question.

steps.question: How do you document the list's footprint so that guests can use it?

a.label: Leave it to the supplier
a.explanation: The auditor is reviewing your restaurant, not the supplier.

b.label: One number for the whole restaurant, no detail
b.explanation: A single number gives the guest no choice to make.

c.label: Mark each wine's origin and packaging, and show a low-footprint choice in every category
c.explanation: Guests can only choose if the information sits where they choose: on the list, per wine.

fail.outcome: The documentation is vague and the auditor says so.

steps.question: Which initiative gives the most environmental credibility?

a.label: Put a green plant in the window
a.explanation: A symbol without substance convinces no one.

b.label: Document the whole list's CO₂ footprint and offer guests a climate choice
b.explanation: Transparency and the guest's chance to make active choices are the core of social and environmental sustainability. Documentation also gives you an edge.

c.label: Buy climate offsets
c.explanation: Offsets do not change what you serve.

d.label: Swap every glass for recycled material
d.explanation: It is a small step compared with what is in the bottles and how they travel.

fail.outcome: The audit notes good intentions and little else.

success.outcome: The auditor singles out the wine list as an example for the village.

staff.outcome: {personal} answers what they can. The audit passes, without praise.

somm-k7.title: Natural wine festival
somm-k7.body: Grythyttan is holding its first natural wine festival. Every restaurant is competing for attention.

steps.question: What is usually meant by natural wine?

a.label: Wine from organically grown grapes, fermented with its own yeasts, with little or nothing added
a.explanation: There is no single legal definition, but natural wine usually means organic or biodynamic grapes, wild yeasts and minimal additions.

b.label: Any wine with a screwcap
b.explanation: The closure has nothing to do with it.

c.label: Wine with no alcohol
c.explanation: Natural wine is fermented and contains alcohol like other wine.

fail.outcome: {personal} cannot explain what the festival is about.

steps.question: How do you serve a cloudy, unfiltered natural wine?

a.label: Tell the guest it is unfiltered, so the haze is expected, and pour gently
a.explanation: Explaining the haze turns a possible complaint into part of the wine's story.

b.label: Say nothing and let the guest think it is faulty
b.explanation: An unexplained haze looks like a fault.

c.label: Filter it through a coffee filter at the bar
c.explanation: It strips the wine of what the producer intended and exposes it to air and paper taste.

fail.outcome: A guest sends the wine back as faulty.

steps.question: How do you position your restaurant during the festival?

a.label: Copy the neighbours' menu
a.explanation: Copying makes you the second choice.

b.label: Take the festival off
b.explanation: You give the village's biggest week to your rivals.

c.label: Cut every price
c.explanation: Price wars give attention to the cheapest, not the best.

d.label: Curate a themed tasting with stories about the producers and terroir
d.explanation: Terroir stories and curated experiences set you apart. Guests pay more for the story behind the bottle, not just the wine in the glass.

fail.outcome: The festival passes, and the crowds go elsewhere.

success.outcome: Your tasting is the one people talk about when the festival ends.

staff.outcome: {personal} keeps the doors open. Some festival guests come in.

somm-k8.title: Allergy crisis
somm-k8.body: A guest reacts to a wine that contained undeclared egg white used for fining. The situation escalates.

steps.question: Why can wine contain egg white?

a.label: It comes from the cork
a.explanation: The cork has nothing to do with egg.

b.label: Egg white is used for fining, to soften tannins and clarify the wine
b.explanation: Fining agents such as egg white bind to tannins and particles, which then settle out. Traces can remain.

c.label: Egg is added for flavour
c.explanation: Egg is not a flavouring in wine. It is a processing aid.

fail.outcome: {personal} does not know where the egg came from. Precious minutes pass.

steps.question: What do you do right now for the guest who is reacting?

a.label: Offer a glass of water and carry on
a.explanation: An allergic reaction can get worse quickly. Water is not enough.

b.label: Take it seriously: stop serving it, ask about medication, and call for medical help if the symptoms are serious
b.explanation: With allergies, act first and ask questions later. Serious symptoms mean calling for help at once.

c.label: Tell them it cannot be the wine
c.explanation: Denying it wastes time and may be wrong.

fail.outcome: The guest is left waiting for help while the room watches.

steps.question: What should the team have done before serving?

a.label: Nothing — it is the producer's responsibility
a.explanation: The guest trusts the restaurant, not the producer. Knowing the list is the team's job.

b.label: Declared every fining agent up front and had alternatives ready for guests with allergies
b.explanation: Social sustainability means inclusion and speaking up first. A responsible sommelier team knows its list and says so before anyone asks.

c.label: Served only natural wine
c.explanation: Natural wine can also be fined. The label 'natural' is no guarantee.

d.label: Asked every guest about allergies when booking
d.explanation: It helps, but it does not replace knowing what is in your own wines.

fail.outcome: The evening ends with an incident report and a shaken team.

success.outcome: The guest is cared for, the list is relabelled the next morning, and the regulars notice.

staff.outcome: {personal} handles the moment, but the question of how it could happen remains.

somm-k9.title: A competition invitation
somm-k9.body: The Swedish Sommelier Association invites a team to the regional championship. It takes five weeks of intensive preparation.

steps.question: What is usually tested in a sommelier competition?

a.label: Only how fast you can open bottles
a.explanation: Speed matters in service tasks, but it is a small part.

b.label: Only knowledge of prices
b.explanation: Prices come up, but tasting, theory and service dominate.

c.label: Blind tasting, theory and practical service in front of a jury
c.explanation: Sommelier competitions combine blind tasting, written or oral theory and service tasks judged live.

fail.outcome: {personal} underestimates what the competition asks.

steps.question: How do you train for the blind tasting?

a.label: Memorise the jury's favourite wines
a.explanation: The wines are unknown in advance. Only skill carries over.

b.label: Read about wine but never taste
b.explanation: Blind tasting is a skill of the senses. It is learned by tasting.

c.label: Taste regularly and systematically as a group, compare notes and learn from mistakes
c.explanation: Regular, structured group tasting builds the shared reference points that blind tasting depends on.

fail.outcome: The team trains without a plan and the weeks slip by.

steps.question: How do you justify taking part to the owner? (Scander et al., 2020)

a.label: It is good PR but gives no real knowledge
a.explanation: PR is a side effect. The knowledge is the point.

b.label: Competitions are for individuals, not teams
b.explanation: What one person learns lifts the whole team.

c.label: It is unnecessary — competitions give no practical knowledge
c.explanation: The research says the opposite: competitions build knowledge that books cannot.

d.label: Competing builds social capital that turns into cultural capital: contact with leading sommeliers, exposure to legitimate judgements of taste and a network that strengthens the restaurant
d.explanation: Scander et al. (2020): sommeliers' skill is built largely through competitions and contact with leading practitioners. One informant describes training with 'well-known sommeliers' who taught him the right words, positioning and style — knowledge that is not in books.

fail.outcome: The owner says no, and the chance passes.

success.outcome: The team comes back with a placing, new contacts and a better list.

staff.outcome: {personal} goes alone, underprepared. It is a lesson, not a result.
